lead: A spark plug seals a small gap inside the combustion chamber and fires a spark across that gap. The spark is timed shortly before top dead centre on the compression stroke. The voltage needed to break the gap is not fixed. It rises with gap size and cylinder pressure, and falls when the electrodes are hot. The ignition coil must supply that voltage with enough stored energy. If the coil cannot, the engine misfires, especially under full load. This chapter explains plug construction, heat range, fouling and the high-voltage pulse path.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the coil, primary current and the collapsing-field idea.

blocks.text: The plug is a metal shell around a ceramic insulator. A terminal at the top takes the high-tension cable. The insulator is alumina ceramic; it holds the centre electrode and carries heat from the tip to the shell. The centre electrode runs through the insulator. Its tip faces one or more ground electrodes fixed to the shell. The shell screws into the cylinder head and gives the earth return. A suppressor seal is a small resistor near the terminal. It limits radio-frequency noise and seals combustion gas. A copper core in the centre electrode carries heat away; platinum or iridium tips resist erosion.

Heat range is the plug's ability to shed heat from its tip to the shell. It is set by the length of the ceramic nose. A hot plug has a longer nose: the tip runs hotter, so it burns off carbon and oil. It suits a cold engine or a lightly loaded engine that would otherwise stay below self-cleaning temperature. A cold plug has a shorter nose: the tip runs cooler and avoids pre-ignition. It suits a hot engine or a high-power engine. The range number alone is not enough; numbering systems run in opposite directions, so match the plug to the engine maker's specification.

The gap is the shortest distance between the centre and ground electrodes. It is set to 0.7–1.1 mm. A gap that is too small gives a weak, short spark; too large a gap raises the firing voltage beyond the coil. Carbon or oil fouling builds a conductive bridge across the insulator or gap. That bridge leaks current before the spark can form.

sections.h3: Firing voltage and the high-voltage circuit

blocks.text: The gas in the plug gap is an insulator until free electrons gain enough energy to ionise it. The voltage at which this avalanche starts is the firing voltage, V<sub>f</sub>. V<sub>f</sub> rises when the gap is wider, because the electric field is weaker for the same voltage. It rises with cylinder pressure, because denser gas has more molecules to ionise. It falls when the electrodes are hot, because a hot surface emits electrons more easily. Typical values are V<sub>f</sub> = 10–35 kV, gap = 0.7–1.1 mm and spark duration = 1–2 ms. A high-compression engine at full load sits near the top of that band.

blocks.where: V₂ is the ideal secondary voltage in volts (V); n is the turns ratio N₂/N₁; V₁ is the primary voltage induced at current break in volts (V), not the battery voltage.

blocks.text: The coil must make V₂ larger than V<sub>f</sub>. The coil stores energy in its magnetic field. At current break the primary voltage rises to V₁, not 12 V, and the secondary gives V₂. A 1:100 coil with V₁ = 250 V gives 25 kV ideal. The high-voltage path is secondary → HT cable → distributor cap → rotor → plug cable → terminal → centre electrode → gap → ground electrode → shell → engine block → earth. Each joint adds loss: rotor gap, cable resistance, suppressor cap, dirt on the cap. The plug sees less than the coil's ideal V₂.

Pulse energy follows the formula below. A coil with 8 mH and 6 A stores 144 mJ. That energy sustains the spark for about 1–2 ms. Too little energy gives a short, weak spark that cannot ignite a lean or turbulent mixture. Too much energy erodes electrodes. The coil therefore needs both enough turns ratio for voltage and enough stored energy for duration.

blocks.where: E is stored energy in joules (J); L is primary inductance in henries (H); I is primary current in amperes (A).

blocks.text: A fouled plug can fire at low pressure and fail at high pressure. At idle the cylinder pressure is low, so Vf is low. At full load the pressure is high, so Vf rises. If the coil's V₂ is already near the limit, the extra few kilovolts decide between spark and misfire. The same logic explains why a worn plug with an enlarged gap misfires first under load; the gap raises Vf. See Chapter 2.3 for how the ECU controls dwell and timing.

figure.caption: Firing voltage rises with gap. The full-load line is a high-compression, high-boost example, so it lies above the light-load line; at gap 0.9 mm (x = 9) it reads 29.8 kV.

spec.aria: Two straight lines show firing voltage rising with spark gap, with the high-compression full-load line lying above the light-load line for every gap.

examples.question: A coil has primary inductance 8 mH and the primary current reaches 6 A before the points open. Find the energy stored. The coil has a 1:100 turns ratio and the primary voltage at break is 250 V. Find the secondary voltage and check whether it fires a 0.9 mm gap on full load using the full-load line.
steps: Convert inductance: L = 8 mH = 8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> H. Primary current I = 6 A.
Stored energy: E = ½ L I² = 0.5 × 8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> × 6² = 0.144 J = 144 mJ.
Turns ratio n = N₂/N₁ = 100. Primary induced voltage at break V₁ = 250 V.
Ideal secondary voltage: V₂ = n V₁ = 100 × 250 V = 25,000 V = 25 kV.
Gap = 0.9 mm = 9 units of 0.1 mm, so x = 9. From the full-load line, V<sub>req</sub> = 10 + 2.2 × 9 = 29.8 kV.
Compare: V₂ = 25 kV is less than V<sub>req</sub> = 29.8 kV by 4.8 kV. The coil cannot fire this gap at full load, so the engine misfires under load.
examples.answer: Stored energy is 144 mJ; ideal secondary voltage is 25 kV; the full-load requirement at 0.9 mm is 29.8 kV, so the coil is short by 4.8 kV and the engine misfires under load.

I = 6.0

print(round(E, 3))
print(round(E * 1000, 1))
n = 100
V1 = 250.0
V2 = n * V1 / 1000.0
print(round(V2, 1))
gap_mm = 0.9
x = gap_mm / 0.1

print(round(Vreq - V2, 1))

traps: Do not multiply the turns ratio by 12 V. The secondary voltage is n times the primary voltage induced at current break; the battery voltage is not present across the primary at that instant.
Do not read the plot's x-axis as millimetres. It is in 0.1 mm steps, so 0.9 mm is x = 9, not x = 0.9.
Higher compression raises firing voltage. It does not lower it, because denser gas has more molecules to ionise.
A hot plug is not a plug for a hot engine. Hot range runs hotter for a cold or lightly loaded engine; cold range runs cooler for a hot, high-power engine.
Suppressor caps and resistor plugs reduce radio noise; they add resistance and secondary loss, not spark energy.

quiz.q: Define the heat range of a spark plug.
quiz.a: Heat range is the plug's ability to shed heat from its tip to the shell and cylinder head, set mainly by the length of the insulator nose.

quiz.q: Why does a hot plug suit a cold engine?
quiz.a: A cold engine keeps the plug tip cool. A hot plug retains more heat, reaches self-cleaning temperature and burns off carbon and oil deposits. It does not overheat because the engine itself is cool.

quiz.q: A coil has turns ratio 80 and primary induced voltage at break 300 V. Find the ideal secondary voltage in kV.
A plug gap is 1.1 mm. Convert it to the plot's units and use the full-load (high-compression) line V = 10 + 2.2x to find the firing voltage.
quiz.a: x = 1.1 mm / 0.1 mm = 11. V = 10 + 2.2 × 11 = 10 + 24.2 = 34.2 kV. This is near the upper limit of the 10–35 kV band, as expected for a high-compression engine at full load.

quiz.q: Why can a plug fire at idle but miss at full load?
quiz.a: Full load raises cylinder pressure, so the firing voltage rises. The coil's maximum secondary voltage is fixed. If V₂ is below the new firing voltage, no spark forms. Electrode temperature and fouling also change the requirement.

quiz.q: Name two secondary losses in a distributor ignition system and state their effect.
quiz.a: The rotor gap and a suppressor cap both add series impedance. They drop part of the coil's secondary voltage before it reaches the plug, so the voltage available at the gap is lower.

quiz.q: What does the suppressor seal in a spark plug do?
quiz.a: It contains a resistor that limits radio-frequency noise and it seals combustion gas from escaping past the terminal.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines now use iridium-tipped plugs and coil-on-plug, so the distributor loss disappears. Lean-burn and high-boost engines push firing voltage toward the top of the 10–35 kV band. Research looks at spark duration, multiple sparks and ion-current sensing. Search terms: spark plug heat range, firing voltage, coil-on-plug, suppressor plug, ion sensing.
